subject: science
objective: Identify the main parts of a typical human (animal) cell, describe the job of each, trace how a cell builds a protein and sends it out, and explain how different human cells have shapes and parts that fit their jobs.
sources: NHGRI Talking Glossary of Genomic and Genetic Terms (https://www.genome.gov/genetics-glossary)
Sender R, Fuchs S, Milo R (2016). Revised estimates for the number of human and bacteria cells in the body. PLoS Biology 14(8): e1002533 (https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533)
misconceptions: Cells are flat, empty bags with a few parts floating in them
All human cells look like the textbook drawing
Every cell has exactly one nucleus
Mitochondria make energy out of nothing
Human cells have cell walls or chloroplasts
The DNA itself leaves the nucleus to build proteins
Organelles really are these colors and sizes
modelLimitations: Two-dimensional, conceptual drawing; not to scale. Ribosomes, vesicles, and pores are drawn far too large.
Colors are added to tell parts apart; real organelles are mostly colorless.
Only a few cytoskeleton fibers, ribosomes, and organelle copies are drawn. Real cells are crowded.
Peroxisomes, intermediate filaments, and many other structures are left out.
The protein journey shows one protein and skips steps such as how its destination is signaled.
Cellular respiration is simplified to 'sugar plus oxygen releases energy'; the first steps actually happen in the cytoplasm.
City analogies are comparisons and break down in places; the lesson says so.
Gallery drawings are not to scale with each other.
